prompt: Ana runs `gofmt internal/tally/classes.go`, with no flags. What happens to the file?
hint: Look at where the formatted text appeared in section 02.

choices.text: Nothing: the formatted version goes to standard output
choices.why: Right. With no flag, `gofmt` prints the result and leaves the file as it was; `-w` is what writes it back.

choices.text: It is rewritten in place, and its name is printed
choices.why: That is `go fmt`, which runs `gofmt -l -w`. Plain `gofmt` writes nothing unless it is given `-w`.

choices.text: It is left alone, and each style problem is reported with its line number
choices.why: `gofmt` is a printer, not a checker: it never lists problems, it prints the file in the one layout.

choices.text: It is renamed to `classes.go.orig`
choices.why: `.orig` appears only in the header of a `-d` diff, as a label. No file of that name is created.

prompt: `gofmt` turned `if status/100==c` into `if status/100 == c`. Why are there spaces around `==` and none around `/`?
hint: In the same file, `float64(n) / float64(s.Lines)` kept spaces around `/`.

choices.text: `gofmt` always writes arithmetic operators without spaces
choices.why: The `Share` expression in the same output has spaces around `/`. The rule depends on the expression, not on the operator.

choices.text: The tighter-binding operator is written without spaces
choices.why: Right. `/` binds tighter than `==`, so it is written without spaces and the eye reads `status/100` as one piece. Alone in an expression, `/` gets spaces.

choices.text: It kept the spacing Ana typed around `/` and only fixed `==`
choices.why: Ana typed no spaces around either operator. `gofmt` decides the spacing from the syntax tree, not from the original.

choices.text: A space after `/` could start a comment
choices.why: A comment starts with `//` or `/*`; a space after a single `/` cannot make one.

prompt: Match each way of running `gofmt` on an untidy file with what it does.
hint: Three flags decide where the result goes; the fourth way uses none.

pairs.right: prints the formatted file to standard output
prints the names of the files that differ
prints a unified diff of the changes
writes the result back and prints nothing

right_distractors: drops the type name from each element of a composite literal

prompt: `go fmt -n ./...` printed the command it would run: `/usr/local/go/bin/gofmt -l ___ main.go main_test.go ...`.
hint: The flag that writes the result back into each file.

prompt: Bruno's editor shows a tab as 2 columns and Carla's as 8. Both open the `Class` struct after `gofmt`, with its comments lined up. What does each of them see?
hint: Indentation and alignment are made of different characters.

choices.text: Lined-up comments for Bruno only, since `gofmt` aligns for 2-column tabs
choices.why: `gofmt` assumes no tab width for alignment: it aligns with spaces, which are one column in every editor.

choices.text: Different indentation, but the columns aligned for both
choices.why: Right. Each field line starts with one tab, which each editor draws at its own width; the padding between name, type and comment is spaces, so the columns survive.

choices.text: Exactly the same thing, because `gofmt` replaced the tabs with spaces
choices.why: `gofmt` indents with tabs: section 02's table shows one tab per level. Only the alignment is spaces.

choices.text: Misaligned columns for both, until each runs `gofmt` with their own tab width
choices.why: `gofmt` has no tab-width setting to run it with, and it does not need one: spaces align the same at any width.

prompt: Why can no `gofmt` setting put a function's opening brace on a line of its own?
hint: Section 03 piped such a function into `gofmt`.

choices.text: The setting was removed in favour of a `.gofmt` file in the module
choices.why: `gofmt` reads no configuration file, and `gofmt -h` lists every flag it has: none of them chooses a style.

choices.text: It is possible with `-r`, by rewriting `{` into a newline and `{`
choices.why: `-r` rewrites expressions, and its output is printed in the same layout. It has no way to express a line break.

choices.text: A line break there ends the statement: a syntax error
choices.why: Right. A newline after `)` ends the statement, so a lone `{` on the next line cannot be parsed: `unexpected semicolon or newline before {`.

choices.text: Only `go vet` may change braces
choices.why: `go vet` reports suspicious code and changes none. The brace position is fixed by the language itself.

prompt: Which of these does `gofmt` leave exactly as you wrote them? Choose all that apply.
hint: Compare the untidy `classes.go` with what `gofmt` printed.

choices.text: A line of 109 characters
choices.why: Yes. `gofmt` never wraps a long line; the `append` line came out on one line.

choices.text: A variable called `n`
choices.why: Yes. Names are untouched; whether `n` is a good name is for the linters of lesson 8.

choices.text: Three blank lines in a row
choices.why: No. The three blank lines after the struct became one.

choices.text: Four spaces of indentation
choices.why: No. Indentation became one tab per level.

choices.text: The wording of a comment
choices.why: Yes. A comment is moved with its code and never reworded or re-wrapped.

prompt: `gofmt -l .` prints nothing, and `gofmt -s -l .` prints `internal/tally/classes_test.go`. What does that tell Ana?
hint: What did `go fmt -n` show that `go fmt` passes to `gofmt`?

choices.text: `go fmt ./...` will shorten the literal on its next run
choices.why: `go fmt` runs `gofmt -l -w` and nothing more, so it never applies `-s`; the literal stays until somebody asks for `-s` by name.

choices.text: The test has a bug that `-s` detected
choices.why: The test passed. `-s` looks for constructs it can shorten without changing what they mean, not for bugs.

choices.text: The file is formatted, but `-s` has a literal to shorten
choices.why: Right. Layout and simplification are separate questions: the `Class` before each element of `[]Class{...}` is correct and redundant.

choices.text: `-s` will change what the test checks, so it has to be reviewed by hand
choices.why: Every `-s` rewrite keeps the meaning: the diff took the type name off four rows and left their values as they were.

prompt: Ana wants to rename `tally.Count` to `tally.Tally` and runs `gofmt -r 'a.Count -> a.Tally' -w .`. What is the state of the module afterwards?
hint: Which occurrences of `Count` are written with a dot in front?

choices.text: Renamed everywhere, since `-r` checks which package each `Count` belongs to
choices.why: `-r` matches syntax and has no types: in section 03 the `a` in `a.Duration` matched `time` as happily as `e`.

choices.text: Unchanged, because `-r` refuses to touch an exported name
choices.why: Nothing in `-r` looks at whether a name is exported; it rewrites any expression its pattern matches.

choices.text: Broken: the calls say `tally.Tally`, the function is still `func Count`
choices.why: Right. `func Count(...)` has no dot, so the pattern does not match the declaration, while every `x.Count` call changes, including any on other packages.

choices.text: Renamed only inside `internal/tally`, where `Count` is declared
choices.why: `-w .` walks the whole module, and the pattern knows nothing about where a name is declared.

prompt: What did `goimports -w` do to the import block of `tools/classes/main.go`?
hint: The block held one package before, and `go build` named nine problems.

choices.text: Sorted `strings` into place and left the rest to the compiler
choices.why: It did more than sort: the build errors were missing and unused imports, and those are what `goimports` fixes.

choices.text: Removed `strings` and added the five packages the file uses
choices.why: Right. `fmt` and `os`, `tally`, and `message` and `language` from `golang.org/x/text`, in two groups, with the unused `strings` gone.

choices.text: Added the missing packages and kept `strings` commented out
choices.why: An unused import is removed outright. The compiler refuses one, so keeping it would leave the file unbuildable.

choices.text: Added `go get` lines for the two modules it could not find
choices.why: `goimports` changes only the Go file. The requirement on `golang.org/x/text` had to be added to `go.mod` with `go get` first.

prompt: Put the lines of the import block in the order `goimports -local example.com/hits` writes them.
hint: Standard library, other people's modules, then yours; sorted inside each group.

prompt: Why did Ana run `go get golang.org/x/text@v0.43.0` before `goimports`?
hint: Where does `goimports` look for a package called `message`?

choices.text: So that `goimports` could find the two `x/text` packages
choices.why: Right. It searches the standard library, the module itself and what `go.mod` requires; a module nobody requires is not a candidate.

choices.text: Because `goimports` downloads nothing and `go get` formats the import block
choices.why: `go get` edits `go.mod` and downloads; it never touches a `.go` file. The block was written by `goimports`.

choices.text: Because `goimports` refuses to run in a module with no requirements
choices.why: It ran fine on files that import only the standard library; the requirement matters only for the packages it has to find.

choices.text: To remove the `// indirect` mark first
choices.why: `go get` added the mark; `go mod tidy` removed it later, once a file imported the module.

prompt: On a team, Davi runs `goimports` on save without `-local`, and Elisa runs it with `-local example.com/hits`. Neither changes any code. What do their commits show over a month?
hint: Run each version over a file the other has just written.

choices.text: Nothing: `goimports` reads `-local` from `go.mod`
choices.why: `goimports` reads no such thing: section 04's first run, without the flag, put `tally` in the same group as `golang.org/x/text`.

choices.text: Build failures, since import order decides which package wins
choices.why: The order of an import block changes nothing about the build; both arrangements compile to the same program.

choices.text: Diffs that move the module's own imports between groups, back and forth
choices.why: Right. Each save rewrites the other's block: Elisa splits a third group out, Davi merges it back. Section 05 puts the flag in one script for this reason.

choices.text: A `gofmt -l .` check that fails on Elisa's files
choices.why: Plain `gofmt` only sorts within groups and accepts either arrangement; it is a `goimports -local` check that would tell them apart.

prompt: A CI step runs `gofmt -l .` alone. A pull request with an untidy file passes it. Why?
hint: Look at the exit status printed after the file name in section 05.

choices.text: `gofmt -l` lists the file and still exits 0
choices.why: Right. Listing is what it was asked to do, so it reports success; the check has to look at the output, as `test -z "$(gofmt -l .)"` does.

choices.text: CI runners use a `gofmt` configured more leniently than a laptop's
choices.why: `gofmt` has no configuration at all. The same version prints the same layout on every machine.

choices.text: `-l` only reads files that changed since the last commit
choices.why: `-l .` reads every `.go` file under the directory, changed or not.

choices.text: It printed to standard error, which CI does not show
choices.why: The list goes to standard output; CI shows it in the log, under a green step.

prompt: With the untidy `classes.go` in the tree, which of these commands exit with a status other than 0? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two tools with the same flags did not agree.

choices.text: `gofmt -l .`
choices.why: It listed the file and exited 0.

choices.text: `test -z "$(gofmt -l .)"`
choices.why: Yes, 1: the captured output was not empty.

choices.text: `gofmt -d .`
choices.why: Yes, 1: `gofmt -d` exits 1 whenever it prints a diff.

choices.text: `goimports -d .`
choices.why: It printed a diff and exited 0, unlike `gofmt -d`.

prompt: With `internal/tally/broken.go` unparseable, Ana runs `out=$(gofmt -l .) && test -z "$out"; echo $?`. What number does `echo` print?
hint: The assignment carries the exit status of the command inside `$(...)`.

prompt: Ana's pre-commit hook passed, yet CI's `check-fmt.sh` failed on the same commit. Which explanation fits the hook of section 05?
hint: What does the hook read: the files on disk, or what was staged?

choices.text: CI has a `gofmt` built with different layout settings from hers
choices.why: There are no layout settings, and the script pins `goimports@v0.52.0` in both places.

choices.text: She fixed a staged file on disk without adding it again
choices.why: Right. The hook checked the tidy file on disk while Git committed the untidy version that was staged; CI checked out what was committed.

choices.text: The hook ran without `-local` and CI with it
choices.why: Both run the same `scripts/check-fmt.sh`, which carries `-local` itself; that is why it is one file.

choices.text: CI also checks `vendor/`, which the hook skips
choices.why: Both run the script on `.`, and `hits` has no `vendor/` anyway.

prompt: A module keeps a deliberately broken `.go` file in `parser/testdata/` as input for a test. Its copy of `check-fmt.sh` now fails with status 2 on every run. What is the right fix?
hint: Which directories does `go fmt ./...` leave out, and why?

choices.text: Delete `|| exit 2` from the script
choices.why: That would also let a real file that does not parse slip through, which is exactly the hole section 05 closed.

choices.text: Name the module's own code directories instead of `.`
choices.why: Right. `testdata/` holds inputs the go command never builds; naming your code's directories keeps the check strict where it should be.

choices.text: Put `// Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT.` at the top so `gofmt` skips it
choices.why: `gofmt` has no exemption for generated files: it reads them like any other, and this one would still fail to parse.

choices.text: Run `gofmt -w` on `testdata/` once, so it stops failing
choices.why: `gofmt` cannot write a file it cannot parse, and fixing the file would ruin the test that needs it broken.

prompt: Git abandons a commit when the executable file `.git/hooks/___` exits with anything but 0.
hint: The hook that runs before Git records the commit.

prompt: Put in order what happened when Ana first committed with the untidy `classes.go`.
hint: From `git commit` to the commit that went through.
items: the script exits 1 and Git abandons the commit
`git add -u` stages it and the commit goes through
